Speed controls

Speed (service tier) handling for gateway and native rows in the Codex desktop adapter: session start versus mid-chat, Flex, unknown tiers and the private tier store.

About 10 min read · 1 sections

On this page
01 Rollback and mixed versions

Part of the Codex app-server adapter.

Gateway discovery retains the provider's public service_tiers, additional_speed_tiers, and default_service_tier fields. The adapter validates them through live discovery and its private offline cache, then exposes the same capabilities in local and connected-machine model/list responses. Native rows retain their original capabilities. No speed tier is inferred from a model name.

Standard remains the default in this installation. Choose Fast only for a model that advertises it; the pinned SDK identifies Fast as priority. Gateway-only preferences restore a saved new-chat default for the exact selected model. An explicit serviceTier or config.service_tier takes precedence, including explicit null for Standard. A model-only preference change clears the preceding model's tier. Resume and fork inherit their chat's tier; new-chat preferences never replace it. A tier the selected gateway row does not offer is handled as the pinned SDK handles it, and the SDK treats opening a session differently from running inside one. Flex is the exception: the SDK keeps and sends it for every model, so the gateway never drops it.

Request What the gateway sends What happens
thread/start, thread/resume, thread/fork naming a tier the row lacks (serviceTier or config.service_tier), or inheriting a chat tier the row lacks serviceTier: null and no config.service_tier The chat starts as Standard, as the SDK does when it builds a session.
thread/resume, thread/fork for a chat whose tier the gateway never read No tier The SDK applies its own default and drops what the model lacks.
turn/start, thread/settings/update, turn/settings/update The request as the caller sent it, whatever the tier The SDK accepts any tier string, keeps it as the chat's chosen tier, and leaves it off the outgoing request while the model lacks it.

At session start the gateway applies a saved new-chat default first and then checks it against the row, so a saved Fast default for a row that no longer offers Fast starts Standard instead of failing. Inside a chat the gateway never sends serviceTier: null for a tier, never clears the chosen tier, and adds no inherited tier. A Fast chat that runs a turn on a Claude row therefore runs that turn as Standard, and the next turn on a Fast row runs Fast again. serviceTierForTurn changes one turn only and never the chat's tier; the gateway maps its legacy value fast to priority. A tier that is not a string is passed through unchanged, and the SDK answers it as invalid parameters. The serviceTierForTurn field exists only on turn/start, so a session start passes it through untouched. Saving a gateway default tier that the chosen row does not offer is the one tier check left: that configuration write fails with error -32002 and asks the user to choose Standard or another model. That check has no Flex exemption: a Flex default can be saved only for a row that declares Flex, as in 0.4.0 (see Rollback and mixed versions). Flex is passed to the provider at session start and inside a chat, as native Codex sends it. The Codex subscription provider forwards it without checking the row's tier list. The Claude and Copilot providers treat Flex as Standard; that handling ships in the same release.

The SDK accepts any tier string inside a chat, including values such as auto, Fast or a very long id. The gateway's private tier record holds only lowercase ids of up to 128 characters that are not auto. For any other tier the gateway records the chat's tier as unknown. It writes this through the same locked, timestamp-ordered path as a known tier: a marker row holding the source time stays under a separate key derived from a hash of the chat id, and the chat's own record becomes a Standard row with the marker's stamp. This build reads a row no newer than its marker as unknown, so a later resume or fork adds no inherited tier, on this connection and on any fresh one, and an older notification that arrives late cannot bring a tier back. Both are ordinary rows in the existing file format, so a 0.4.0 build still reads the whole file. It never looks the marker up and finds the Standard row, so after a rollback a fresh 0.4.0 process can fork the chat and change its model; with no record it would refuse both with -32002. The row and the marker are evicted together and count as two rows. A marker also wins over a non-Standard row that falls inside its uncertainty window, because a 0.4.0 build wrote that row without knowing the watermark. A newer Standard row from a 0.4.0 build is trusted over the marker, and it keeps the marker's window, so a late non-Standard notification is still rejected. A marker that outvotes a 0.4.0 row keeps that row's window too. A tier the store can hold that is chosen later replaces the marker. Such a tier never fails a settings notification or a resume, and recording it makes room like any other write. When a peer connection has marked the chat unknown, this connection also stops forwarding the tier it held, whether its own notification was rejected as older or its resume was in flight.

Each dropped tier is recorded as a service_tier_dropped telemetry event, only after the SDK accepted the request and only when its answer shows the chat started as Standard. A loaded chat with another subscriber ignores the override on a resume and answers with the tier it kept, and no drop is recorded then. See diagnostics for its fields.

The pinned SDK does not restore speed from saved history. The gateway therefore keeps public per-chat model/tier metadata in its own private state, scoped to the original native home. Fresh connections reread this record. Runtime settings are recorded from the SDK's applied settings notification, not its queued update ACK. SDK source timestamps reject delayed settings events. Private revisions prevent an older resume reply from replacing a newer choice. Conflicting events stamped in the same millisecond resolve conservatively to Standard; an explicit confirmed SDK snapshot can establish the current choice again. Clock uncertainty never restores Fast from an uncertain older notification. The adapter passes the known parent tier explicitly when forking because the SDK otherwise uses executor defaults. If the gateway never read the parent's tier, the fork carries no tier and the SDK chooses its own default. The SDK's returned tier is authoritative. Resuming an already-loaded chat keeps its loaded settings even when resume parameters request another tier; change it through thread/settings/update. A cold resume can apply an explicit override. Temporary active-turn tiers remain separate from the chat default. Gateway executors enable the SDK's Fast feature when their validated catalog offers priority. Native feature flags and configuration files retain their values; enabling that private capability does not select Fast automatically.

A loaded Fast chat that switches to a model without Fast keeps its Fast tier, and the SDK runs the new model's requests as Standard. The private record of that chat holds Standard from the switch on, because its row does not declare Fast; the SDK's Fast returns to the record when the chat is on a Fast row again. A connection that cannot determine the saved tier sends none, so a model change never clears or invents it. Reasoning effort is independent of speed.

Rollback and mixed versions

The 0.4.0 adapter checks a chat's saved tier against the tiers its row declares and refuses with -32002 when the row lacks it. During an upgrade, 0.4.0 adapter processes keep running beside this build on the same state files until the desktop restarts its CLI, and a rollback leaves 0.4.0 in charge of every saved chat. The rule that keeps both safe:

What is written What this build writes
A chat's tier in the private tier store (session-start answer, applied settings notification) The tier only if the chat's row declares it in its catalog metadata, with no Flex exemption. Any other storable tier is recorded as Standard. A tier the store cannot hold stays the unknown marker described above.
A saved new-chat default (config/value/write, config/batchWrite) Only a tier the selected row declares, or Standard. Anything else fails with -32002.

A Flex chat, a Fast chat that moved to a row without Fast and a saved default therefore resume and run turns under 0.4.0 without an error, provided the chat is not loaded in an SDK that a 0.4.0 client shares with this build. A loaded chat keeps its Flex, or the Fast it had before moving to a row without Fast, inside the SDK, and the 0.4.0 client checks that tier against the row and can refuse with -32002. To recover, choose Standard in the 0.4.0 client, or reopen the chat from 0.4.1. The cost is that a chat on a row without Flex declared does not carry Flex across a resume or fork: the SDK still keeps and sends Flex while the chat is loaded, but the next session start inherits Standard from the record. Nothing else changes: the record is read only at session start, where a tier the row lacks already starts the chat as Standard (Flex was the one exemption), and inside a chat the gateway forwards tiers untouched and never applies the record. The test app-server-0-4-0-rollback.test.ts runs every row and saved default this build writes through the 0.4.0 checks, which app-server-0-4-0-tier-check.ts copies verbatim from release commit 4a8bb9e, including the chats on a tier the store cannot hold (auto, Fast).

The compaction recovery file is bounded differently. This build keeps 4096 chats and evicts the oldest instead of failing. After a rollback with a full 4096-row file, 0.4.0 still updates the chats already in it, but it refuses a row for a new chat and warns that compaction recovery metadata is unavailable for it.

Claude rows offer Fast when Claude's own model list marks the model as supporting fast mode (currently the Opus models). Fast turns on Claude Code's fast mode for that request, which Claude bills to the account's usage credits. Discovery refreshes this capability with the rest of the catalog, so every connected machine sees the same option.

The current Copilot CLI does not offer a selected-model Fast tier. Its four configured models expose no speed options. A direct Fast request is rejected before starting the CLI. The integrator-only Auto Fast API is a different route and is not enabled by this installation.

Installing updated adapter code preserves open apps and running services. Already-loaded older adapters need their next normal launch to expose these new fields. Catalog updates use the usual live discovery path after activation.

The circular arrow in the model control is Reset to default. It chooses a default power preset; it does not fetch a fresh model catalog. That preset can belong to the native account, so a gateway chat cannot always apply it. Provider switch refusals use an application error code rather than the app's configuration validation code, avoiding a false warning that config.toml is broken. Explicit saved model defaults are also reflected in the catalog's default flag. The app's power presets can still exclude custom aliases, so this flag does not permit a loaded chat to change providers.

The adapter fetches the inference host's public catalog when listing models and starting gateway work. A changed catalog starts a fresh gateway executor for new chats. Loaded native and gateway chats keep their connections. To select a newly added model in an older loaded gateway chat, close and resume that saved chat, or start a new one. Ephemeral chats cannot be resumed after their executor exits.

Gateway model names remain listed during a connection outage, including after an adapter restarts. A private cache stores the last valid public model rows, scoped to the local gateway port and a hash of its client token. Selecting a gateway model still requires fresh discovery. An unavailable gateway returns application error -32001 before creating a chat or using the native account. When the connection recovers, normal discovery reloads the catalog without an app restart. Invalid or differently scoped caches leave native models usable.

The desktop query itself has a five-minute cache and refetches on focus in the installed build. Catalog changes require no app restart after initial activation, but immediate visible picker updates are not guaranteed. There is no fabricated account-change notification to force a refresh.

Gateway executors use a private configuration home and share native chat storage. They do not copy the primary auth file. See architecture for configuration isolation, catalog generations, and failure recovery.
